lessons.title: Pick-and-roll anatomy
lessons.objective: Name the ball handler, screener, roll, pop and slip.

payload.prompt: What is a pick-and-roll?

options.text: A ball handler uses a screen set by a teammate, then either drives or the screener rolls to the basket.
A player without the ball sets a screen for a teammate cutting to the basket.
The referee calls a pick foul followed by a jump ball.

explanation.correct: Right. A pick-and-roll is the most common offensive action: screen, then roll or pop. It is run hundreds of times a game.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A pick-and-roll is when a screener sets a barrier for the ball handler, then moves (rolls or pops) to get open or be involved in the play.

payload.prompt: What does rolling mean in a pick-and-roll?

options.text: The screener moves toward the basket after setting the screen, looking for a pass.
The screener dribbles backward to create space.
The ball handler bounces the ball on the ground.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The roller moves toward the basket and is often open for a quick pass or layup.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rolling is the screener's movement toward the basket after the screen is set, an easy catch-and-finish spot.

payload.prompt: Match each pick-and-roll action to what the screener does.

pairs.definition: The screener moves toward the basket after setting the screen, looking for a pass from the ball handler.
The screener steps out to the perimeter for a jump shot after the screen is set.
The screener breaks to the basket without actually setting the screen, using surprise timing.

distractorDefinitions: The ball handler fakes and goes the other direction.
The screener sets another screen at the same time.

explanation.summary: Roll is toward the basket; pop is out to shoot; slip is breaking early for a layup.

payload.prompt: Order the steps of a pick-and-roll from start to finish.

items.text: The screener moves to set a barrier for the ball handler.
The ball handler dribbles toward the screen and uses it to create space.
The screener either rolls, pops or slips based on the defense.
The ball handler either drives, shoots or passes to the screener.

explanation.correct: Right. The sequence is: pick, attack it, screener decides their move, then the action happens.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The pick comes first, then the handler attacks it, then the screener reacts, then the play concludes.

lessons.title: Coverages: drop, hedge, switch, blitz
lessons.objective: Tell drop, hedge, switch, blitz and ice apart.

payload.prompt: Match each pick-and-roll defense to how it works.

pairs.definition: The screener's defender backs away from the screen, letting the ball handler take a shorter shot.
The screener's defender steps out briefly to slow the ball handler, then recovers back.
The two defenders trade assignments, one guarding the new opponent.
Both defenders attack the ball handler immediately, trying to force a turnover.

distractorDefinitions: The ball handler's defender traps on the sideline.

explanation.summary: Drop stays home; hedge recovers; switch trades; blitz attacks aggressively.

payload.prompt: What is the risk of playing drop defense on a pick-and-roll?

options.text: The ball handler gets space for a pull-up jump shot.
The screener rolls unopposed for an easy layup.
The offense cannot get open for any shots.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Drop defense leaves space for the ball handler to shoot, especially dangerous if they can shoot threes.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Drop defense gives up the pull-up shot because the ball handler has space to shoot.

payload.prompt: Match these pick-and-roll adjustments to their meanings.

pairs.definition: Force the ball handler to one side so the screener's defender can help without opening the roller.
The ball handler's defender goes around the back of the screen without fighting over it.
The ball handler's defender fights through or over the screen, staying attached.

explanation.summary: Ice forces to the side; under goes around; over fights through.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Hedge and recover. Do not give up the three.

payload.question: What is she calling?

options.text: A pick-and-roll defense where a defender briefly steps out to slow the ball handler then recovers back to the screener.
Let the screener roll unopposed to the basket.
Switch defenders on the screen.
Foul the ball handler immediately.

payload.translation: She is calling a defensive tactic where the screener's defender steps out to show pressure, then slides back before the ball handler can shoot a three.

followUps.line: Yeah, that is quick and controlled.
followUps.why: You recognize that hedging is about timing and recovery.

followUps.line: Who recovers back to the roller?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking who needs to be ready for the pass.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Hedge means step out and step back quickly; do not overcommit.

lessons.title: Reading a coverage live
lessons.objective: Pick the best action against each coverage as it happens.

payload.prompt: What should the ball handler do if the defense hedges tight on a pick-and-roll?

options.text: Quick pass to the screener who is rolling or popping, since the defense is committed elsewhere.
Stop dribbling and pass out to reset the possession.
Take a long jump shot immediately.

explanation.correct: Exactly. When the defense hedges, they leave the screener open, making the quick pass the best option.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Against a hedge, the screener is usually open after the defense steps out, so a quick pass is the right read.

payload.prompt: What is a short roll in a pick-and-roll?

options.text: A quick pass to the screener who has only rolled a short distance from the screen, before the defender recovers.
The screener dribbles only a few dribbles before shooting.
A roll that does not go all the way to the basket.

explanation.correct: Right. A short roll is passing to the screener early in their movement, before defense can catch up. High-percentage pass.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A short roll is a quick touch pass to the roller before the defense relocates, often in the mid-range.

payload.question: What does that mean?

options.text: The ball handler quickly recognized how the defense was playing the pick-and-roll and made the right pass or shot.
She looked at a defensive scheme diagram.
She memorized the defense's playbook.
She guessed where to pass.

payload.translation: She is saying the ball handler instantly saw how the defense was positioned (hedging, switching, etc.) and made the right decision—pass, shoot, or drive.

followUps.line: Yeah, that is why she is the point guard.
followUps.why: You recognize that reading coverage is a key playmaking skill.
A good follow-up asking about the outcome of the smart read.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Reading coverage means seeing the defense and reacting correctly, not literally looking at diagrams.

lessons.title: Handoffs and the DHO
lessons.objective: Explain a dribble handoff and why teams love it.

payload.prompt: What is a dribble handoff (DHO)?

options.text: A ball handler hands the ball directly to a moving teammate, creating separation.
A pass made after a player has dribbled and stopped.
Passing the ball to a teammate on the bench.

explanation.correct: Right. A DHO is a quick, direct hand-to-hand transfer while the receiver is moving. Teams love it because it is fast and creates separation.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A dribble handoff is when a ball handler hands the ball (not passes) to a teammate who is moving to meet them.

payload.prompt: Handler stops dribbling, passes to a cutting teammate. Is this a DHO?

scene.alt: A ball handler stopping and passing to a cutting teammate.

explanation.correct: Right. A DHO happens while dribbling; the receiver meets the dribbler and takes the ball directly. If the dribbler stops, it is just a pass.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A dribble handoff requires the dribbler to still be moving; a pass after stopping is not a DHO.

payload.prompt: On a half-court diagram, tap where the ball handler and receiver meet to complete a dribble handoff.

diagram.alt: A basketball half-court showing handoff spots.

explanation.correct: Good. Handoffs can happen anywhere on the floor, but common spots are the top, wing and elbow.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Handoffs happen on the perimeter—top of key, wings and elbows are typical spots.

lessons.title: Post entries and split cuts
lessons.objective: Follow a post entry and the split cut that follows.

payload.prompt: What is a post entry?

options.text: A pass to a big man in the low or high post, setting up a post-up or drop-off pass.
A pass out of bounds to restart play.
A pass that leads to a transition break.

explanation.correct: Right. A post entry initiates play through a big, often leading to a post-up, pass-out or split cut.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A post entry is a pass to a big man in a scoring position, usually low or high post.

payload.prompt: What is the elbow in basketball terms?

options.text: The corner where the free-throw line meets the lane, a key spot for shooting and passing.
The point where a player fouls using their elbow.
The joint in a player's arm.

explanation.correct: Right. The elbow is part of the high-post area, a sweet spot for shooting, passing and driving.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The elbow is the corner of the free-throw line and lane, a key location in the high post.

payload.prompt: On a half-court, tap the high-post areas (near the free-throw line extended).

diagram.alt: A basketball half-court showing high-post spots.

explanation.correct: Yes! The high post is the free-throw line area—elbows and top of the key. The paint below is the low post.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The high post is the area near the free-throw line: elbows and top of the key, not the paint.

payload.prompt: If a post entry goes to the right elbow, tap where the split cutter comes from (down the middle).

diagram.alt: A basketball half-court showing split cut paths.

explanation.correct: Right! The split cutter comes down the middle between the post defender and the post player.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A split cut comes down the middle, exploiting the gap when two defenders collapse on the post.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Post entry, then kick it out.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Pass to the big man in the post, and if the defense collapses, pass the ball back out to a shooter.
The ball goes directly out of bounds.
Physically kick the ball to a teammate.
Skip the post and shoot immediately.

payload.translation: She means the offense should get the ball into the post, and then if the defense helps, kick it out to an open shooter on the perimeter.

followUps.line: Yeah, that is the drive-and-kick from the post.
followUps.why: You recognize the offensive action of entering the post and finding shooters.

followUps.line: Who is open on the wing?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking who the kick-out pass should go to.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Post entry is passing to a big; kick-out is passing back to a shooter when help comes.

lessons.title: Pindowns, floppy and getting shooters open
lessons.objective: Recognize the screens that free a shooter running off the ball.

payload.prompt: What is a pindown screen?

options.text: A screen set for an off-ball player above them on the court, freeing them to move down or away from it.
A screen for the ball handler at the top of the key.
Holding a player to the rim.

explanation.correct: Right. A pindown is set by a player above (toward the sideline) a teammate, creating space to cut or get open.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A pindown is a screen set above an off-ball player, creating movement and separation.

payload.prompt: What is a stagger screen?

options.text: Two screeners setting consecutive screens for an off-ball player, creating a path or multiple options.
A single player setting unbalanced screens.
Screens set at different times during the same possession.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Stagger screens are two in a row—the player uses one, then the other, creating confusion and space.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A stagger screen is two consecutive screens set for one player, one after the other.

payload.prompt: Match each off-ball screen action to what it creates.

pairs.definition: A screen set above an off-ball player, freeing them to cut or move away from the basket.
Two consecutive screens for an off-ball player, creating multiple paths to get open.
A screen that pushes a player out to the three-point line for a catch-and-shoot.
Two bigs setting screens on opposite sides, giving the ball handler options to attack either way.

distractorDefinitions: A screen that immediately results in a foul.
A screen set in the restricted area.

explanation.summary: Pindown frees a player to move; stagger is two screens; flare moves to three; floppy gives two-way options.

payload.prompt: On a half-court, tap the three-point corner where a flare screen moves the shooter.

diagram.alt: A basketball half-court showing flare screen destinations.

explanation.correct: Yes! Flare screens move the shooter to the corner or wing three-point line for an open shot.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A flare screen moves a shooter to the perimeter (corner or wing) to get them open for a three.

lessons.title: Isolation and mismatch hunting
lessons.objective: Explain why offenses force switches and attack the weak defender.

payload.prompt: Do you attack the mismatch or reset the possession?

situation.narrative: A ball screen created a switch. Your team's quick small guard is now guarding a slow big. You have the ball.

facts.label: Guard's defender
facts.value: A bigger, slower defender now guarding your quick ball handler

facts.label: Opportunity
facts.value: The mismatch is obvious; your guard can attack with a dribble drive

options.label: Attack the mismatch
options.consequence: Drive the ball, get a quick layup or draw a foul. The big cannot defend a penetrating guard.
considerations: The big is slower than your guard
A guard attack on a big often draws fouls

options.label: Reset and run a set
options.consequence: Safe but wastes the mismatch. You miss free points.
considerations: You will need another play later

payload.expertNote: Mismatches are hunting opportunities: a guard on a big should attack with a drive or shot. A big on a guard should post up or shoot three. Always punish the mismatch.

payload.prompt: Should you run screens to create a switch?

situation.narrative: Your ball handler is an elite scorer, but the defense is staying attached and not switching. You can run screens to try to create a switch.

facts.label: Your strength
facts.value: Elite scorer, can beat any defense one-on-one

facts.label: Defense strategy
facts.value: Staying attached, fighting through screens without switching

facts.label: Your goal
facts.value: Get your scorer space or create a mismatch

options.label: Run screens to hunt a switch
options.consequence: Force the defense to switch and create a mismatch you can attack. Your elite scorer gets space.
considerations: Switches are inevitable if you keep screening

options.label: Iso the scorer without screens
options.consequence: Elite scorers can still create, but you miss the mismatch opportunity.
considerations: Your scorer might beat them anyway
Harder for your scorer, easier for the defense

payload.expertNote: Mismatch hunting through screens is intentional strategy: keep screening until the defense breaks and switches, then attack the weaker defender.

payload.prompt: What is isolation efficiency?

options.text: How efficiently a team scores when one player attacks one-on-one with teammates staying out of the way.
How efficient a team is on their own possessions.
A measure of how isolated a defender is.

explanation.correct: Right. Isolation efficiency tracks how many points per possession a team gets in iso situations, a key stat for star scorers.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Isolation efficiency is the points per possession a team or player gets in one-on-one scenarios.

payload.prompt: Why might a team choose to switch everything on defense?

options.text: To avoid mismatches and prevent guards from scoring in the post or shooting threes, even if it creates other mismatches.
Because they want to allow all cuts.
To make the offense score faster.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Switch-everything is a trade-off: you eliminate specific bad mismatches (guard in post) but create others (big on guard). Teams choose based on their personnel.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Teams switch everything to prevent certain types of mismatches, even if it creates different ones.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They keep hunting us on the switch. We need to go big.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The offense keeps creating switches to get a mismatch (like a small guard defending a big), and the defense needs to switch everything or go to a bigger lineup.
They should buy the offense a bigger ball.
The offense is bigger than the defense.
They need to build a larger gym.

payload.translation: She is saying the offense is intentionally forcing switches to create favorable mismatches. The defense should respond by going to a larger lineup to prevent getting beaten by size or speed mismatches.

followUps.line: Yeah, they are targeting our small lineup.
followUps.why: You recognize that mismatch hunting exploits the opposing team's weaknesses.

followUps.line: Who do we need to bring in?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking which larger player should enter the game to fix the mismatch.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Hunting switches means running screens to force switches and create mismatches. Going big means using taller players to avoid getting exposed.

lessons.title: Late-clock offense
lessons.objective: Understand the 14-second reset and what teams do with 6 seconds left.

payload.prompt: With 8 seconds on the shot clock, should you shoot or dribble? Tap when to shoot.

explanation.correct: Right. With 8 seconds or less, you should take a shot or create separation for one; very little time remains.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. With only 8 seconds left, you are in late-clock offense and need to shoot soon.

payload.prompt: When an offensive rebound is grabbed in the NBA, what happens to the shot clock?

options.text: It resets to 14 seconds, giving the offense a second chance with less time.
It resets to 24 seconds, the same as the start of a possession.
It stops and does not reset.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The 14-second reset is a key rule: grab an offensive board, get 14 seconds to shoot again. Great chance to score.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Offensive rebounds reset the shot clock to 14 seconds in the NBA, giving a quick second chance.

payload.prompt: What is a bailout shot?

options.text: A late-clock desperation shot taken when the play breaks down and time is almost out.
A free throw awarded when a team fouls out.
A shot that rescues a losing team.

explanation.correct: Right. A bailout is just a rushed attempt when the clock is running out and nothing else is working. Often a three-pointer or a long two.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A bailout shot is a desperation attempt at the end of the shot clock when the offense has not created an open look.

payload.prompt: A play breaks down and the ball handler is at half-court with 4 seconds on the shot clock. When should they shoot?

explanation.correct: Right. With only 4 seconds left from half-court, shoot immediately or it is a shot-clock violation.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. With 4 seconds left, any delay might mean the ball does not get off before the clock expires.

payload.prompt: If an offensive rebound happens with 3 seconds left on the shot clock, how much time do you get to shoot?

explanation.correct: Exactly. The shot clock resets to 14 seconds after an offensive rebound, no matter how much time was left.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. All offensive rebounds reset to 14 seconds in the NBA.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: With very little time on the shot clock, one player is attacking one-on-one to score or create a shot before time expires.
The game is ending immediately.
A player is isolated from their teammates.
The offense is playing too slowly.

payload.translation: She is saying with only a few seconds left on the shot clock, the team is running an isolation play where one player takes the shot one-on-one. That is the last chance to score in this possession.

followUps.line: Yeah, it is hero time. All or nothing.
followUps.why: You recognize that late-clock isos are high-stakes, one-shot attempts.
A good follow-up asking if the iso player got space for a shot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Late-clock iso is a last-second offensive attempt when time is nearly gone.
